title: Metric Learning and Contrastive Learning
learning_outcomes: Explain the role of metric learning and contrastive learning in a PyTorch workflow.
Apply a small example of metric learning and contrastive learning and interpret the output.
Identify a relevant limitation, debugging check, or reproducibility concern.

content.intro: Metric Learning and Contrastive Learning: Advanced learning paradigms reuse the tensor/autograd foundation but optimize different objectives, such as reconstruction, adversarial generation, similarity, rewards, or multiple tasks. In this lesson, use a small example to make the inputs, outputs, and boundary conditions explicit.
content.why_it_matters: Specialist architectures are useful when their assumptions fit the problem; they are optional paths rather than a requirement that every learner master every model family. For this lesson, focus on similarity embeddings and the evidence you can collect from a controlled example.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the learning objective and data contract. Choose losses and evaluation methods based on what the model should learn, not only on the architecture’s name. The source topics for this lesson are: Similarity embeddings, Positive and negative pairs, Contrastive objectives. Keep each topic connected to a checkable input/output behavior.

content_blocks.title: Read the example
content_blocks.text: Identify each model component, what target or signal supervises it, and what output or metric can validate the concept on a small example. The example is a teaching-scale check, not evidence of a trained model score or a hardware-independent performance claim.

items.title: Similarity embeddings
items.text: Trace token IDs, sequence length, padding/causal masks, and prediction targets so the model only uses information available for the task.

items.title: Positive and negative pairs
items.text: Connect this topic to the lesson workflow: Start with the learning objective and data contract. Choose losses and evaluation methods based on what the model should learn, not only on the architecture’s name. Write down the expected behavior and test it on a small, inspectable input.

items.title: Contrastive objectives
items.text: Start from the learning objective and identify its input, target or feedback signal, loss, and evaluation method before scaling the architecture.

items.title: Triplet-loss concepts
items.text: Connect the quantity to the model objective and update order; track it over steps and change one training setting per experiment.

items.title: Embedding evaluation
items.text: Choose a metric that matches the task, compute it on the intended split, and inspect representative errors before interpreting one aggregate score.

content_blocks.title: Guided PyTorch example
content_blocks.code:
import torch
a = torch.tensor([1.0, 0.0])
b = torch.tensor([0.9, 0.1])
print(torch.nn.functional.cosine_similarity(a, b, dim=0).item() > 0.9)

content.task: Try it yourself: Choose one specialist family, sketch inputs/components/loss/output, and build a small shape-valid model stub or toy objective. Record the observed result and one limitation; do not report an unrun training or performance result as measured.

troubleshooting.symptom: A tensor operation raises a shape, dtype, or device mismatch.
troubleshooting.check: Print .shape, .dtype, and .device for each input. Resolve the mismatch intentionally instead of changing dimensions blindly.

troubleshooting.symptom: The example fails because an optional package or accelerator is unavailable.
troubleshooting.check: Check the installed PyTorch/package versions and device availability. Use the official installation selector and run the CPU-compatible path where appropriate.

troubleshooting.symptom: The result differs across runs or machines.
troubleshooting.check: Fix the seed where useful, record versions and inputs, and document operations that remain nondeterministic or hardware dependent.

common_mistakes.problem: Relying on assumptions instead of inspecting the data or output.
common_mistakes.why: Many ML failures come from incorrect shapes, labels, preprocessing, or execution mode rather than a syntax error.
common_mistakes.fix: Inspect representative inputs and add assertions for the expected shape, dtype, range, or behavior.

common_mistakes.problem: Mixing training-time behavior with inference-time behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Dropout, normalization, gradient tracking, and optimizer updates can change how a model behaves.
common_mistakes.fix: Do not compare specialist models using a metric or training signal that does not match their intended objective.

common_mistakes.problem: Using a current or experimental API without recording its version assumptions.
common_mistakes.why: Hardware support and ecosystem APIs can change independently of the core package.
common_mistakes.fix: Pin compatible dependencies, record the environment, and test after upgrades.
